analysis.one_liner: Bars the largest app stores from forcing developers to use their own payment systems or favoring their own apps.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill to curb Apple and Google's app store rules died in committee without ever getting a vote, despite 20 House cosponsors and a Senate companion that cleared the Senate Judiciary Committee.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have set rules for app stores run by companies with more than 50 million U.S. users — in practice, Apple's App Store and the Google Play Store. It would have barred those companies from forcing app developers to use their in-house payment systems, from punishing developers who offer cheaper prices elsewhere, from collecting developers' nonpublic data to build competing products, and from ranking their own apps above rivals in search results. It would also have let users install apps from outside the official store. The FTC, the Justice Department, and state attorneys general could enforce the rules, and injured developers could sue for triple damages. The bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: App developers — from small studios to large companies like Spotify and Match Group — who could avoid app-store commissions of up to 30% by directing users to outside payments, and consumers who could see lower app and subscription prices and more choices for how they install software.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits app stores with more than 50 million U.S. users from requiring developers to use the store's own in-app payment system or from penalizing developers who offer different pricing elsewhere [S2] [S3].

Bans covered companies from using nonpublic business data collected from third-party apps to compete with them, and from unreasonably ranking their own apps or their partners' apps above rivals in search results [S2] [S3].
Requires app store owners that control the operating system to let users set third-party apps and app stores as defaults, install apps outside the official store, and delete preinstalled apps [S3].
Gives the FTC, the Justice Department, and state attorneys general enforcement power, and lets injured developers sue for triple damages and attorney's fees [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Apple and Google, whose app stores take commissions of up to 30% on many transactions and whose control over what software runs on their phones would be curtailed; the cost would fall partly on their shareholders and partly be passed through to app store economics generally.
analysis.who_pays_short: Apple and Google's app store businesses

drawbacks.text: Apple and other critics argued that forcing sideloading and outside payment systems would weaken the security, privacy, and malware screening that app stores provide to ordinary users; the bill includes a safety exception, but only if the company proves its practices are consistent, non-pretextual, and narrowly tailored, which would be litigated case by case [S3].

The rules would apply by size to essentially only two companies, which supporters defended as targeting gatekeeper power but which opponents called regulation aimed at specific firms rather than a general rule of competition [S2] [S3].

Opening the platform could reduce the app store owners' revenue from commissions, some of which is used to fund free tools, security updates, and developer services; the bill did not require replacement funding for those functions [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers and developers, the likely gains are lower prices, more payment and installation choices, and a check on two companies that control nearly all app distribution on phones. The most serious honest objection is security: a device manufacturer can no longer be the sole gatekeeper for what software users install, and the bill's safety exception depends on after-the-fact proof rather than upfront screening. On balance the bill was a targeted competition rule aimed at a specific bottleneck in the digital economy, not a broad rewrite of antitrust law.

outcome.mechanism: The House Judiciary Committee never scheduled the bill for consideration, and it sat at the subcommittee level until the Congress ended on January 3, 2023, so it never received a vote in either chamber.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 9, 2022 by Rep. Hank Johnson of Georgia with bipartisan original cosponsors including Republicans Ken Buck and Madison Cawthorn, and was referred to the House Judiciary Committee [S1] [S3].
It gathered 20 cosponsors, 14 Democrats and 6 Republicans [S4].
On November 1, 2022 it was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Antitrust, Commercial, and Administrative Law, and no further action was recorded [S5].
The Senate companion bill advanced out of the Senate Judiciary Committee, but no chamber ever voted on the Open App Markets Act before the 117th Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Apple and Google are better off: their app stores continue collecting commissions of up to 30% and controlling app distribution on their phones with no new legal limits. Developers who pushed for the changes got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Apple and Google's app store businesses

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan: 20 House cosponsors split 14 Democrats and 6 Republicans, and the Senate companion was sponsored by a Democrat and a Republican.

industries.note: The bill targeted the two companies that together control nearly all app distribution on U.S. smartphones, ending mandatory use of their payment systems (which carry commissions of up to 30%) and their power to block outside app installation. Their interest in keeping that system runs against consumers and developers who pay the commissions.

industries.industry: App developers (from small studios to Spotify and Match Group)
industries.note: Developers could direct users to outside payment options with lower fees, communicate directly with users, and sue for triple damages if the store owners violated the rules. Their gain in lower fees largely flows to lower prices and more choices for consumers.

industries.industry: Alternative app stores and app distributors
industries.note: The bill requires operating system owners to allow users to install third-party app stores and apps, opening a market those companies were previously excluded from.
